"A lemma. In math. My daughter taught me that word. It's a helper proposition." He shrugged. "You prove the little thing so the big thing follows."

Kate pulled up, set the brake, looked at him. The cones sat behind her, aligned, untouched, and she felt nothing like triumph. "So what's the big thing?"

"That's for you to say." He checked his mirror. "Ramp. Let's go."

The on-ramp to Route 9 rose between a guardrail and a concrete wall scrawled with a faded telephone number for a towing company. Errol had her stop at the top, engine idling, turn signal ticking. Traffic moved in the right lane, steady and indifferent. A truck came first, its container painted with the logo of a furniture company, then a gap that looked, to Kate, large enough until she began calculating whether the car behind the gap would have to slow down.

She waited. The truck passed. The gap passed. The next car honked, though it had not needed to slow at all, and Kate's hands tightened on the wheel.

"He could have moved over," she said. "There was nobody in the left lane. He had room."

Errol tapped the dashboard. "Who has to yield here?"

Kate looked at the ramp, at the merge sign, at the stream of headlights. Something in the phrasing of the question made her feel she was being handed the answer rather than asked for it, which annoyed her, and the annoyance was useful because it made her actually look. The cars on the highway weren't changing their speed for anyone. They didn't have to. She was the one on the ramp. She was the one joining.

"I do," she said slowly. "Traffic already on the highway has the right of way. So I'm the one who has to adjust. Fit the gap instead of expecting them to make one." She exhaled. "That's so backwards. It feels like the powerful one should be the generous one."

"It's not a moral system," Errol said. "It's just who's already there." He paused. "Though I'll tell you, plenty of licensed drivers never learned it, and it makes them pernicious. They merge like the world owes them a lane, and everybody brakes, and that's how you get those backups with no accident anywhere."

Kate watched the traffic again, this time the way she watched the cones: not as obstacles but as a pattern with a logic to it. A sedan passed. Then a gap opened, real this time, wide and unhurried, and she brought the car up the ramp at speed, matched the flow, and slid into the space with a smoothness that surprised her more than the parking ever had.

"That," Errol said, "was the big thing."

They did it four more times. On the third, the gap was smaller and she had to speed up more than she liked, but she found herself reading the traffic differently, less like a petitioner at a door and more like a swimmer timing waves. Still, something about it sat uneasily with her on the drive back to the lot. She understood the rule now, could recite it, and yet she kept thinking about the driver who had honked, and about the truck driver who hadn't moved over, and about how a rule could be correct and still feel cold. She didn't say any of this. She suspected the feeling would fade, and she wasn't sure she wanted it to.

In the lot, Errol had her park once more, between the cones, under the humming light. She executed it in three movements, tire to curb, centered, done. She sat with her hands on the wheel.

"Can I ask something that isn't on the test?"

"You can ask."

"If I have to fit the gap, and everyone has to fit the gap, then where does it start? Somebody has to let somebody in sometimes, or nobody new ever gets on the road."

Errol chewed his gum and looked out at the empty lot for a while. "Somebody does," he said. "Usually. Not because they have to."

Kate nodded, not sure whether she had been answered or trusted with an open question, and pulled the key from the ignition. Outside, the cones stood exactly where she'd left them, two pale shapes waiting for the next lesson.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: A launch velocity v at an angle θ above the horizontal splits into a horizontal component v cos θ and a vertical component v sin θ.
story:
The projectile launcher at the science museum stood at the end of the physics hall, between a Foucault pendulum and a case of cracked meteorites. Felix had walked past it a dozen times on school trips, but today he was here alone, with a notebook and a problem his professor had left on the board as a dare: a ball launched at twenty degrees above the horizontal, and how far it would go. He had until Monday to answer, and the museum's launcher, with its adjustable angle and its measured range markings on the floor, was the only way to check himself.

His little sister Priya had insisted on coming, mostly for the gift shop, but she'd settled onto the bench beside the exhibit with a slushie the color of an accident. "You're going to fire that thing at kids," she said. "I can feel it."

"Twenty degrees," Felix said. "Barely off flat." He'd worked the problem twice on the train and gotten two different answers, which did not augur well. The first time through, he'd drawn his triangle and labeled the side along the angle as the vertical component, the way it looked in his sketch, and calculated that the ball would climb almost straight up, hang for an absurd time, and land nowhere near the floor markings. The second time he'd swapped the labels and gotten a low, fast arc that seemed far too ordinary for all the algebra it had cost him.

He set the launcher's dial to twenty degrees, loaded the yellow ball, and pressed the release. The ball shot out in a flat, shallow curve, struck the floor at the eight-meter mark, and bounced toward a toddler, whose father fielded it with practiced calm and rolled it back. "Sorry," Felix called. The father waved it off, smiling, and Felix noticed Priya already retrieving the ball before he'd finished apologizing, handing it back to him with the solemn efficiency of a surgical nurse.

He crouched over his notebook. The flight had been low and long. That meant the horizontal part of the launch velocity was the big one at a shallow angle, and the vertical part was small. He looked at his two attempts. In the first, he'd claimed that a launch at twenty degrees would send the ball nearly straight up, which the exhibit had just disproven in front of a toddler. He crossed it out with a stroke hard enough to dent the page.

A museum docent drifted by, the kind of man who read your body language before speaking. "Trouble with the trig?" he asked, and Felix, caught, admitted it. The docent didn't launch into anything. He just tapped the corner of Felix's drawing where the angle sat and said, "Horizontal is cosine, vertical is sine," and moved on toward the pendulum, as if the sentence were no heavier than a coat he'd set down.

Felix sat with it. A launch velocity at an angle above the horizontal split into two components, and the split wasn't his to choose: the horizontal piece was the velocity times the cosine of the angle, the vertical piece the velocity times the sine. At twenty degrees, cosine was large and sine was small, hence the flat, fast, honest arc he'd just watched land at eight meters. His mix-up had reversed the two, predicting that a nearly flat launch would climb like a fountain, which the floor, the toddler's father, and his own crossed-out page all quietly contradicted. He rewrote the problem cleanly, separating the components into two columns the way the docent's sentence had split them in his head, one column for sideways and one for up.

But the range he calculated came out half a meter short of the eight-meter mark, and no amount of rechecking his arithmetic closed the gap. He tried a stoicism he didn't quite feel, telling Priya it was fine, it was close enough, and Priya, who had watched him erase and rewrite three times, said, "It's not fine, you made that face." She was intransigent about the face. He laughed, then leaned down and looked along the barrel: the launcher sat at the height of his knee, not at floor level, and his notebook assumed the ball started from the ground. Some of the mystery was that, maybe, or maybe air, or maybe the dial was a degree off. He wrote beside his answer, "This part I still don't know," and underlined nothing.

The hall was emptying, the pendulum ticking its slow circle, and the docent was locking a supply cabinet near the entrance. Priya stood, draining the last of her slushie, and nodded at the launcher. "One more," she said. "Full power. Angle's your choice."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: On the practical driving test in Great Britain, a candidate passes with no more than 15 driving faults and no serious or dangerous faults.
story:
Carter had the test booked for Friday morning, and by Wednesday he had clipped the curb outside the leisure centre four times, each time with the same instructor in the passenger seat saying nothing at all.

"You're allowed to say something," Carter said, easing out of the space for the fifth attempt.

"I'm allowed," Priya said. "Whether it helps is a different question." She had her own reasons for the silence, though she hadn't shared them: she needed to log forty hours of instruction before her own assessment as an approved instructor, and Carter was hour thirty-one, and if he passed first time, word would get around the sixth form that she was the one to book with. "Again. Full lock, then look at where you want the back wheel to end up, not at the curb."

The car swung in. The rear tyre kissed the kerb with a sound like a knuckle on a door.

Carter sat with his hands on the wheel and tried to work out what he actually believed about mistakes. His father ascribed every setback to a single cause, always one, whether it was the wrong boots or the wrong attitude or the wrong manager. His mother apportioned blame in careful fractions, a bit of weather, a bit of tiredness, a bit of the road. Two systems, both confident, neither ever tested against anything that mattered. He had grown up between them without deciding, and now the decision was nine o'clock Friday, at a test centre car park in Rainham.

"Is that it, then?" he asked. "If I do that on Friday, is that the whole thing over?"

Priya tilted her head. "What do you actually know about how they mark it?"

"Everyone knows. You hit the curb, you fail."

"Everyone," she said, "or the people who failed and told you about it?"

He didn't have an answer, which was itself a kind of information. That night he looked it up himself, scrolling on his bed while his mother watched the late news downstairs. On the practical driving test in Great Britain, a candidate passes with no more than fifteen driving faults and no serious or dangerous faults. He read it three times. Fifteen. He had been driving as though the whole thing turned on a single touch of rubber against stone, and the margin was fifteen wide. He texted Priya: "did you know it's fifteen driving faults?" She replied with a thumbs up and nothing else, which he chose to find funny rather than insulting.

The next morning they went on the dual carriageway for merging practice, which was worse than parking in every way that mattered to him. The slip road was recalcitrant, short and curved, and the traffic in the left lane had a way of sitting exactly where his mirror said he needed to be. He stalled once, indicated once when he shouldn't have, and merged the third time with a lorry so close behind that Priya finally spoke without being invited.

"Speed up. You're joining, not asking permission."

"I was being careful."

"You were being slow in the one place where slow is dangerous." She said it without heat, and he understood it as the corollary of the curb: the fault isn't the mistake itself, it's what kind of mistake it is, and where, and what it does to other people. Fifteen driving faults were room to be imperfect. A serious or dangerous fault, one, and it was over. He tried to hold both ideas at once: be generous with your own small errors, and ruthless about the ones that could hurt somebody.

On Friday morning the sky was the flat grey of a photo taken without intending to. The examiner was a compact woman with a clipboard and a manner that suggested she had already reviewed his file and found it adequate. The parallel park came early, outside a parade of shops, and he felt the rear wheel brush the kerb, a small definite touch, and his whole body went cold.

"Continue when you're ready," the examiner said.

He pulled forward, corrected, straightened, and carried on, because he had decided the night before what to believe: that a touched kerb, by itself, was a driving fault, and that he had fourteen left, and that the way to honour that margin was not caution but attention. The rest of the route went through two roundabouts, a hill start, and the same slip road from practice, empty this time, where he accelerated hard and slotted into the lane like a letter into a slot.

Back at the test centre, the examiner filled in her sheet for a long time. Carter watched the pen and tried not to ascribe meaning to its speed or its pauses.

"Throughout the test," she said, "you accumulated four driving faults."

Carter waited, because there was more, and because he knew now that waiting was part of it.

"No serious faults. No dangerous faults." She looked up. "I'm pleased to tell you that you've passed."

He laughed once, too loud for the little car park, and Priya, waiting by her own car with her phone in her hand, raised it and took a picture of him standing there with the pass certificate, which she would later post, though he would not learn that until the evening.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: In C major the dominant seventh chord is G7, made of the notes G, B, D and F, and it pulls strongly toward the C major chord.
story:
The concert hall had a rehearsal room off the west corridor, and the woman at the desk had told Logan he could use it until six, when the cleaners came through. He set his staff paper on the upright piano's music stand and sat down. He had four days to finish sixteen bars for the youth composition prize, and the eleven bars he had written so far were, he knew, polite. They moved where they were supposed to move. They ended phrases the way his theory textbook said phrases could end, and nobody would object to any of it.

That was the problem. Two hundred other seventeen-year-olds would submit something polite.

He played the melody through from the top. It lived in C major, mostly stepwise, with one leap he liked, a jump up to E in the fifth bar that he'd written at midnight and had not touched since. Under it he had written simple chords: C major, then F, then C again. The last bar was a C major chord, a whole note, the obvious home. His teacher at school, Mr. Heyer, had looked at his draft on Tuesday and made a sound that was hard to read, somewhere between approval and apology. "It's correct," Heyer had said, which exculpated nobody, least of all Logan, since correctness was exactly what he was afraid of.

At four o'clock a girl opened the door without knocking. She had a viola case on her back and a lanyard that said orchestra librarian, which meant she belonged in the building and he did not. "Sorry. I left my folder in here this morning." She went to the chair by the window and picked up a black folder, and then, instead of leaving, she looked at his staff paper. "Is that for the composers' thing? The prize?"

"Yeah. Sixteen bars. It's due Friday."

"Can I hear it?"

He almost said no. Instead he played it, all eleven bars and then the ending he'd sketched, the C major chord landing flat and final and a little bit dead. He kept his hands on the keys and waited.

"It just stops," she said. She said it without cruelty, the way you'd say a shelf was crooked. "The tune's fine. The ending kind of lies down."

"I know." He had known it for three days, and hearing it said aloud in a rehearsal room made it worse, because it was now a fact and not a suspicion. She sat down on the piano bench's far end, still holding the folder, and he noticed she wasn't leaving, and he noticed he didn't mind.

"Play your last four bars again," she said. "And when you get to the chord before the end, add an F."

"Add an F to what?"

"Whatever chord you're playing. G, F, whatever's there."

His second-to-last bar had a G chord, a plain triad, G, B and D, holding for two beats before the final C. He played it again and added the F on top, a fourth voice stacked high in his right hand, and then the last bar, the C major chord.

The ending worked. It didn't just work; it pulled. The F sat in the chord like a weight on the edge of a shelf, and the final C major chord arrived as if it had been asked for. He played the two bars again, then again, then the whole last line, and the girl nodded once, the way librarians nod when a book turns out to be where it should be.

"What is that?" he said. "The chord with the F in it."

"Dominant seventh," she said. "G, B, D and F. In C." She stood up and slid the folder under her arm. "My theory teacher calls it the chord that wants to go home. I have to get to rehearsal." She left the door half open behind her, and from down the corridor he could hear an orchestra tuning, all those strings sliding toward a single A.

He sat with it. He wrote the four notes into the second-to-last bar, stemmed and beamed properly, the F on the top space of the treble staff where it belonged, and then he stared at the chord and tried to decide what he thought. Part of him wanted to believe the trick was enough, that one altered chord could exculpate eleven polite bars. Another part of him, the part that had written the leap to E at midnight, suspected that a strong ending bolted onto a timid piece was a kind of lie, and also that the leap and the chord were doing the same job from opposite directions, one by surprise and one by inevitability. He was not sure which he trusted more, or whether a good melody needed both.

He worked backward from the new chord. The bar before it had been another C major, which now sounded like arriving early, so he changed it to F, and the bar before that he left alone. He crossed nothing out; he wrote the revisions in pencil above the old chords, so the page held both versions at once, the page itself equivocal, and he decided he liked seeing the choices rather than hiding them.

At ten to six the cleaner knocked and pointed at his watch. Logan gathered the pages, played the last two bars once more with the soft pedal down, and heard, from the corridor, the orchestra stop mid-phrase. Then, a few seconds later, they started the passage again.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: With typical use, about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined birth control pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed.
story:
Jeremy got roped into it through the Yearbook Club, which was itself a mystery, since he had joined the Yearbook Club to take photographs and hide behind the camera. But Ms. Adeyemi had asked for two students to train as peer health educators, and Priya had volunteered him with the breezy cruelty of someone who knows you cannot refuse in front of a teacher. So on a Tuesday in November he found himself in a conference room at the county clinic, across from a nurse named Ruth, learning to explain consent, contraception, and how to get tested for infections, in that order, because, Ruth said, the order is the point.

"This is not a lecture you memorize," she told him and Priya. "It's a conversation you practice." She slid a plastic model of an IUD across the table, then a package of pills, then a paper cup, for reasons that never became clear. Jeremy took notes anyway. He liked notes. Notes were an encapsulation of a subject into something he could control, and this subject felt like the opposite of controllable, full of body parts and laws and things his mother would want to discuss in Portuguese so the neighbors couldn't follow.

The trouble began, as trouble did, with Marcus. He had come along because the clinic offered free smoothies to student volunteers, an arrangement Ruth described as "a bribe we are comfortable with." During the contraception session, Ruth spent five full minutes on setting a daily phone reminder for the pill, then another five on linking it to something you already do, like brushing your teeth. Marcus raised his hand like they were still in a classroom. "It's one pill," he said. "How hard can it be to remember one pill?"

Ruth didn't answer. She had this policy, Jeremy learned, of letting silence do her work, and she turned her palm toward Jeremy as if handing him the question like a baton.

Jeremy looked down at his notes, where he had underlined a statistic twice. "With typical use," he said, "about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined birth control pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed." It came out flatter than he wanted, like a weather report. Marcus blinked at him. "That's not zero," Jeremy added, and heard his own voice do the thing Priya called his lawyer voice, the one he used when he was assembling a position out of parts he hadn't fully tested yet. "It's not a big number either. That's what typical use means. Real people, real life, sometimes forgetting."

"Seven out of a hundred," Marcus said slowly, as if tasting it. "So the reminder is the whole ballgame." He got out his phone and set an alarm right there, titled it something Jeremy couldn't see, and Ruth permitted herself a smile the size of a comma.

The consent part was harder, and Jeremy understood, in a small cold way, that it was harder because it wasn't about remembering. Ruth had them practice saying "Are you still good with this?" out loud, to each other, in a fluorescent-lit room, while Marcus cracked jokes to keep from dying of embarrassment, and Jeremy laughed and also thought about last spring, about Dana Reiss at Kai's party, about how he had asked and she had said yes and how he still replayed the asking to check whether the yes had been a yes or an exit with better lighting. He had never landed on an answer. He suspected there wasn't a clean one, that the question itself was the thing you kept carrying.

On the Thursday of the actual presentation, Jeremy stood in front of a classroom of juniors with Priya at the whiteboard and his notes face-down on the desk, because he'd decided the notes were a crutch, then picked them up again, because he'd decided that was vanity. He explained the clinic's walk-in hours. He explained that testing was confidential and mostly a swab or a urine cup, and a boy in the second row said "that's it?" with such genuine relief that a girl near the window laughed and the whole room loosened. When Jeremy got to the pill, he repeated the statistic word for word, seven in a hundred, and watched four students take out their phones, or their friends' phones, on the spot.

Afterward Priya said he'd been good, actually, and he wanted to burnish that compliment into something official, a title, a line on a college application, proof that the afternoon had turned him into a certain kind of person. But walking out past the trophy case, past his own blurred photo from the soccer season he'd quit, he understood he didn't know yet what kind of person it had turned him into, only that the question Dana's face still asked him was not the same as the one in his notes, and the notes could not answer it.

Marcus caught up with him at the buses, holding his phone up like a trophy. The alarm had a name after all. It just said "Jeremy."

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote: 35 senators voted to convict, one short of the two-thirds needed.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and Lucas had claimed a folding chair near the back so he could see everyone at once. He was there for his civics teacher, who had assigned him to transcribe the public comment session for the class newsletter, and he had promised himself he would only observe. Observation, his father liked to say, was how you kept your opinions intact. Lucas had opinions. He had spent the whole drive downtown defending the presidential system to his father, who had grown up under a parliament in Jamaica and called Congress "a machine for making kings every four years."

The councilwoman at the microphone table introduced the evening's main item: the town was voting on whether to petition the state for a new emergency water ordinance, and because the county executive had threatened to ignore it, the discussion kept sliding into a fight about what should happen to a leader who refuses to go. "If she won't resign," a man in a plaid coat shouted, "then what? We just wait her out?" Someone near the front said that in a parliament they'd have a vote of no confidence and she'd be gone by Friday, and Lucas felt his ears go hot, because that was his father's argument arriving in a Kentucky gymnasium wearing someone else's voice.

He wrote it down in his notebook, and under it, in smaller letters, he wrote the counterargument he'd been carrying around since September: that fixed terms protect you from the mob, that a president answers to voters on a schedule and not to whoever happens to hold the majority that week. He had a fact for this. He'd found it in the library two nights ago while avoiding his chemistry textbook, in a chapter about Andrew Johnson. In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Johnson by one vote: thirty-five senators voted to convict, one short of the two-thirds needed. He had copied the numbers onto an index card because they felt like evidence, though he hadn't yet worked out of what.

When the public comment period opened again, a girl from the community college stood up, someone Lucas half-recognized from the debate team, and made the parliament case cleanly: the majority picks the head of government and can withdraw that choice, so power stays close to the people who granted it. Lucas's hand went up before he had decided to raise it. He heard himself say that removal by majority alone means a government can fall over a bad week, and then he said the thing on his card. "In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote. Thirty-five senators voted to convict, one short of the two-thirds needed." He said it like a closing argument.

The girl didn't answer right away. She looked at the card in his hand, at the tremor in it, maybe, and something in his certainty began to feel thinner to him even as he stood there holding it. One vote. A president had come that close to removal and had survived it, and which side of that story you stood on depended entirely on whether you thought the bar was a shield or a wall. If the Senate had needed only a majority, Johnson would have been gone. If a parliament had faced him, gone. The same man, the same misconduct, opposite outcomes, and neither system had been designed with him in mind.

"Thank you for the history," the girl said, "but my question is whether you'd want it easier or harder." The room had gone quiet in the way rooms do when an argument becomes interesting, and Lucas understood that his fact didn't answer her question at all. It only sharpened it. He had brought the card here as a verdict, and it had turned metamorphic in his pocket, reshaping itself under pressure into a question instead.

"I used to think harder was obviously safer," he said. The words came out slower than he'd planned, and he watched the councilwoman stop shuffling her papers. "A high bar means removal is rare, and rare means stable. But one vote short also means one senator decided, and I don't know if I trust one senator more than half the legislature." He could hear his father clearing his throat somewhere in the row behind him, and he did not turn around. "I think I want it hard, but not this hard. Or maybe I want it hard and I just don't like who it saved."

A man near the door laughed, not unkindly. "That's the most honest thing anyone's said tonight." Lucas sat down, and his father's hand landed briefly on his shoulder, saying nothing, which between them was a concession of some size. The councilwoman called the next speaker, an old woman who wanted to talk about the aquifer, and the room tilted back toward water. Lucas opened his notebook and began to transcribe her remarks, his pen moving, the index card still on his knee, thirty-five and thirty-four sitting side by side in his handwriting, the one vote still undecided, as far as he was concerned, between them.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Dividing a large batch into shallow containers helps it cool quickly in the fridge, because a deep pot of hot food stays warm in the middle for hours.
story:
The list on the fridge had begun as his mother's handwriting and was slowly becoming his own. Gavin stood in the kitchen on Monday morning with a legal pad, dividing seven dinners into proteins, vegetables and grains, because in nine days she was flying to Phoenix for a month of radiation and he would be the only one feeding himself and his younger sister, Nora. He had watched her cook for eighteen years without once learning how it was done, and now the omission felt like a debt called in.

She had left him a letter, because she left everything important in letters. "The trick isn't cooking," she had written from her hospital bed, the penmanship wavering. "It's Sunday. Cook once, portion it out, and the week takes care of itself. Buy the chicken when it's on sale. Your father used to say stagflation ruined groceries, but honestly groceries were always trying to ruin us." At the bottom she had added, "Feed Nora something green at least twice. She'll pretend she hates it. She doesn't."

He drove to the supermarket with the list torn from the pad and discovered that planning on paper and shopping in aisles were two different intelligences. Four chicken thighs became eight because they were cheaper per pound that way; the onions came in a net bag he hadn't budgeted for; he stood in the grain aisle long enough for the overhead music to cycle twice, holding rice against his internal image of the week, unable to decide whether he was being thrifty or just cheap. In the car he called Nora and read her the plan, and she said the word "hedonistic" with admiration for the Tuesday lasagna, which he took as a compliment even though she'd meant it about the cheese quantity.

The real education happened on Thursday at the community kitchen on Vine Street, where he'd signed up to volunteer because a woman named Priya had told him they'd teach anyone to cook in bulk. They did. A volunteer named Marcus had left a steel pot of lentil soup on the counter, big enough to bathe a toddler in, and Priya wanted it in the walk-in before the evening crowd arrived at six. Gavin went to lift it and understood immediately that carrying forty quarts of hot soup anywhere was a plan for disaster. Priya didn't lecture him. She just slid a stack of shallow deli containers down the counter and started ladling, and so he ladled too, filling the flat tubs two inches deep, snapping lids, stacking them on the shelf. When he touched one a few minutes later it had gone cool at the sides, and he thought of his mother's stockpot at home, which sat steaming on the stovetop for what seemed like half the evening after dinner. He said, "So a big deep pot of hot food stays warm in the middle for hours." Priya nodded without looking up from the ladle. "That's why we split it. Shallow containers, it cools fast."

On Saturday he ran the whole system alone. Nora slept until eleven, so he shopped solo, came home with bags whose weight he felt in his forearms, and took over the kitchen. He roasted the chicken, simmered the rice, sweated onions until they turned translucent and sweet. Steam rose from the pot and made the window above the sink undulate with condensation, the backyard blurring and re-forming behind it like something seen through water. He portioned everything into the shallow containers he'd bought with his own money from the restaurant supply store, labeled them with masking tape, and lined them along the fridge shelf like a small civilization providing for itself.

The deadline pressed on him because his mother flew out Monday and he had promised her one full week of meals, visible and countable, before she left. Sunday evening she came home from her pre-flight appointments tired and thin, and he made her sit at the table while he reheated the chicken and the rice. She ate slowly, watching him move around her kitchen with an expression he couldn't read at first, then chose to read as pride because it was kinder to both of them.

"It's good," she said. "You put thyme in this."

"Priya's idea. Well, partly." He sat down across from her and turned his fork over. "I don't know if I'm actually going to keep doing it, when you're back. I like the planning. I'm not sure I like the part where you eat the same thing Thursday that you made Sunday." It was the first honest sentence about the project he'd said aloud, and she received it without argument, which was her way of saying it was allowed.

Monday morning he drove her to the airport with Nora asleep in the back seat, and when they got home the kitchen was quiet and the containers were still lined up on the shelf, labeled in his own handwriting. Nora stood in front of the open fridge, squinting at the tape. "Which one's dinner?"

"The curry," he said, and reached past her to pull it out.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: Melvyn Leffler's A Preponderance of Power, which won the 1993 Bancroft Prize, argued US leaders pursued national security through dominance of the postwar world.
story:
Blake had been sent to his grandfather's house for the week with instructions from his mother to get some fresh air, which meant, in practice, that he sat at the kitchen table with his laptop open and the back door propped to the garden so the air could reach him. The essay was due Friday: compare two historians' explanations of the Cold War. He had Gaddis, the long peace, the idea that containment had been a patient and mostly rational project. What he didn't have was a second view worth setting against it, and the library copy of the book he wanted had been checked out by someone named T. Alvarez who was evidently in no hurry.

His grandfather came through the kitchen with a watering can and paused at the table. "Still the war that never happened," he said, peering at the screen. "My father used to call it that. He was inure to the fear by the end, I think. You can't duck under a desk every week for years without the fear just becoming weather."

"Did he think it was worth it?" Blake asked. "The whole standoff."

His grandfather considered the watering can as if it might answer. "He thought the Russians were run by an autocrat and we weren't, and that settled most of his questions. It doesn't settle mine." He went out to the tomatoes, and Blake wrote none of it down, then wished he had.

The problem with Gaddis, as far as Blake could tell from three afternoons of reading, was that Gaddis made the American side look almost inevitable, the way a well-taught math proof looks inevitable, so that by the end you forgot anyone could have chosen differently. Blake needed the other thing, the counterweight, and he found it that evening in the bookshelf in the front room, between a water-stained atlas and a box of expired seed packets. His grandfather had been a history teacher before retirement, and the shelf held the evidence: paperbacks swollen with age, a few hardcovers with library-sale stickers. Blake pulled one down because the spine said A Preponderance of Power, and he liked the weight of the word preponderance without quite knowing what it promised.

The book was by Melvyn Leffler, and inside the cover, in his grandfather's handwriting, was a note from 1993: Bancroft Prize, do not lend. Blake carried it to the kitchen and read the first long chapter straight through while the tea went cold. The argument, as he assembled it in the margin of his notebook, was not that American leaders were fools or villains but that they had pursued national security through dominance of the postwar world; they wanted a preponderance of power, enough of it that no rival could imagine challenging them, and that want had its own momentum. Where Gaddis saw patience, Leffler seemed to see appetite dressed as patience. Where Gaddis saw a response to Moscow, Leffler saw plans that would have made sense even if Moscow had been quieter.

"So you found it," his grandfather said, coming in for his glasses. He picked up the book, turned it over. "Cost me a week's wages when I bought it, and I was impecunious enough that my wife made me take it back. I didn't, obviously. It's the best thing on the shelf."

"Which one's right?" Blake asked.

"That's the wrong question, and I'm not going to answer the wrong one for you." His grandfather put the book down, squared to the table's edge, a habit of a man who had spent decades squaring things to edges. "Leffler won the Bancroft for it, which tells you the profession took it seriously. So did Gaddis. Two serious books that disagree. Your job is the disagreeing part, not mine."

Blake sat with both books open side by side until midnight, and the disagreeing turned out to be harder than the reading. On the Marshall Plan, on the atomic monopoly, on almost every fork in the road, the two men looked at the same documents and told opposite stories, and Blake could not find a fact that decided between them. What he could find was a way to hold them: that the Americans believed they were being careful and were also, at the same time, building an empire of sorts and calling it caution, and that maybe both descriptions were true the way his grandfather's father and his grandfather could both be right about the same decades. He drafted a paragraph saying so, then deleted the last sentence because it sounded more certain than he felt.

In the morning his grandfather found him asleep on the couch with both books open on his chest. He lifted them off, marked Blake's place in each with a seed packet, and set them on the table side by side. "Not lending," he said quietly, to no one.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: German capitalizes every noun, not only names, which helps a reader of a German article spot the nouns in a sentence at a glance.
story:
The article lay flat on the table between them, and Isabella kept her finger pressed on the first line as though the words might scatter if she let go. Der Senat plant, die Wohnungsgesellschaft zu expropriieren. She knew "plan," or thought she did, and "Wohnung" she had memorized that morning, apartment, but the last word sat there like a locked drawer.

"Again," said Marta. "From the top."

They had claimed the corner by the periodicals on a Tuesday in late June, three days before the placement interview that would decide whether Isabella spent her first college semester in the beginners' German stream or the intermediate one. Marta was already intermediate. Marta had a mother in Hamburg and a confidence that Isabella both borrowed from and resented, depending on the hour.

Isabella read the sentence aloud. Her pronunciation came out half Spanish, half guesswork, and she stumbled where the sentence refused to break where an English sentence would. "The Senate plans, the housing society, to expropriieren."

"You can't leave half of it in German."

"I can if I don't know it."

"Then guess. What's the context?" Marta tapped the photograph above the headline, an apartment block with sheets hung from windows, letters stenciled onto the fabric. Isabella looked at the block, at the marching capitals scattered through the paragraph, and felt the unfairness of it. English gave you lowercase words and let you drown quietly. Here every third or fourth word stood up and shouted its first letter.

"Why do so many of them start with capitals?" she said. "Is it a newspaper thing? Like headlines?"

Marta shrugged. "They're nouns. All of them, every noun. Names too, but it's not just names, it's every single noun in the whole language, from Banane to Regierung."

Isabella stared at her. She looked back at the sentence and the capitals rearranged themselves in her vision. Der Senat plan(t), die Wohnungsgesellschaft zu expropriieren. The Senate. The housing society. The subjects and objects of the sentence had been standing in plain sight the entire time, wearing bright hats, and she had been reading past them as though they were decoration. She ran her finger down the paragraph and counted: capital, capital, lowercase verb, capital. The sentence's skeleton was visible before she understood a word of its flesh.

"Wait," she said. "So I can find the nouns without knowing any of them."

"That's the cheat code, yes."

"Why didn't you say that an hour ago?"

"You were busy being tragic about the articles."

Isabella went back to the beginning and read again, slower, and this time she marked the nouns with the side of her pencil. Der Senat. Die Wohnungsgesellschaft. She still didn't know what the society did, but the word "Expropriierung" appeared twice more, once in a quotation, and the photograph gave her the rest. A city government taking housing away from a company, tenants holding sheets printed with NEIN. She knew the shape of the story even where she didn't know its words.

"Now summarize," Marta said. "Aloud. In German, three sentences, then English so I know you're not hallucinating."

The first attempt collapsed on the second sentence. Isabella had the nouns and no verbs, a story made entirely of its capitalized bones, and she said so, and Marta laughed in a way that was not unkind. On the second attempt Isabella got through it: The Senate plans something to the housing society. Many people are against it. The decision comes later. Her German was flat and childish, a summary a seven-year-old might give, and she could hear it, and she kept going anyway.

"English," Marta said.

"The city government is considering expropriating the big housing company. The tenants have been organizing for months. Nobody's agreed on what it would do to the housing supply." She paused. "The article says the company's spokesman is sanguine. I think. He says everything will stay as it is."

"He says the throughput of renovations would collapse, actually."

"What does that even mean?"

"Fewer apartments fixed per year. It's in the third paragraph, you skipped it."

She had skipped it. Isabella went back and found the sentence, long and nested, verbs stacking up at the end like cars braking too late. But the nouns still announced themselves, and she located the word, Durchsatz, riding on its capital D, and she understood that she would not understand it, not today, and that the placement interview on Friday would not wait for her to understand everything. She could read the bones of any German sentence put in front of her. She could not yet read the marrow.

Marta checked her phone and started stacking the dictionaries. Isabella copied the article's headline into her notebook, capitals and all, then read the first sentence one final time, aloud, alone, her voice low under the periodicals sign.

"The third paragraph," she said. "Tomorrow. You're not leaving until I get the third paragraph."

Marta shouldered her bag. "Bring the sheets photo. I'll bring a German who argues."

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: Many parliamentary systems separate the head of state, such as a monarch or ceremonial president, from the head of government, while in the United States the president is both.
story:
Xavier spread the photocopies across the long table by the library window, weighting the corners with a mug he wasn't supposed to have brought past the front desk. On the left lay a diagram of Westminster, its arrows looping from the legislature to the cabinet and back. On the right, a diagram of Washington, its arrows running stubbornly in one direction, from the ballot box to the Oval Office and stopping there. He had a debate in eleven days on whether it was easier to fire a leader in London than in Washington, and so far his answer was a shrug he could feel in his shoulders whenever anyone asked him about it.

He had claimed the table at four o'clock, when the after-school crowd thinned. Now the light through the window had gone the color of weak tea, and the asceticism of his setup, one pencil, one legal pad, no laptop, felt less like discipline and more like penance. He copied arrow for arrow, and the copying itself began to teach him something. In the parliamentary sketch, a leader could fall when the arrows turned against him, the same body that had made him could unmake him. In the presidential sketch, the arrows only bent around impeachment, a slow and clumsy thing, and otherwise pointed at a fixed date four years out.

"You're in my spot," a voice said. A girl about his age stood with a stack of returns, a lanyard marking her as a shelver. She didn't move to claim the spot, though; she leaned over the diagrams instead. "School thing?"

"Debate. Parliamentary versus presidential. How they pick a head of government and how they get rid of one." He tapped the right-hand page. "I know this one. We vote for the president directly-ish, and basically the only ways out are the election, the Twenty-Fifth Amendment, or impeachment, which almost never works."

"And the other one?"

"That's where it gets slippery. The parliament picks the prime minister, and parliament can also vote to pull the plug. No waiting for a fixed date. But I keep mixing up the pieces, because some of those countries also have a king."

"A king," she repeated, delighted, as if he'd confessed something. "My cousin asked me that last month when we were volunteering at a polling station. This voter, an old guy, points at the news on her phone and says, why does England have both a king and a prime minister? She told him the king's the boss. Then she told me later she made it up."

"She made up a whole layer of government," Xavier said.

"She didn't know. Neither did I."

Xavier looked down at his diagram and felt something shift, the way a word you've mispronounced for years suddenly sounds wrong. He had been drawing one box at the top of the parliamentary system and labeling it PRIME MINISTER, as if it were a mirror image of PRESIDENT, and the two were not mirror images at all. "Wait," he said, and pulled the pencil across the page. "Many parliamentary systems have two people up there. The monarch or a ceremonial president is the head of state, and the prime minister is the head of government, the one who actually runs things. In the United States, the president is both. Both jobs, one person." He said it twice in his head to make sure he hadn't scrambled it, then checked the diagram's fine print and found the same distinction, in italics, near the bottom where he'd skimmed past it.

"So when the old guy asked about the king," the shelver said, "the answer was that the king isn't the boss at all."

"Right. The king is the, the ceremony of it, and the prime minister is the machinery." Xavier contextualized it for her out loud, pointing at Washington: "Think of it as one person here wearing two hats that those countries split between two." She nodded slowly, the way people nod when a shelf finally holds.

He wrote a question on the legal pad and underlined it: does splitting the jobs make it easier or harder to remove the real leader? The arrows suggested easier, since the prime minister stood or fell with parliament. But then he circled the word SUGGESTED and wrote UNSURE beside it, because he'd read enough debate transcripts to know that what a diagram implied and what a country did were different animals, and he had eleven days, not eleven weeks, to find out which was truer. It was an evanescent kind of certainty, anyway, the kind that dissolved the moment you asked it to survive a cross-examination.

The shelver gathered her returns and balanced them against her hip. "Good luck," she said. "If you lose, tell them the king did it."

He laughed, and after she'd gone he sat a while with the light fading on the two uneven stacks of paper, then drew a third diagram beside the other two, blank except for two boxes at the top and a question mark between them. He wrote at the bottom, in small letters, STILL OPEN, and left it there, side by side with the rest, before packing the mug into his bag.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: The 'file drawer problem', a term coined by psychologist Robert Rosenthal in 1979, describes studies with null results going unpublished, which makes the published record look more positive than the evidence.
story:
The writing club met in a spartan classroom at the end of the science wing, six folding chairs around a table that still bore someone else's chemistry notes. Ava arrived first, as she always did, and spread her materials in front of the chair she thought of as hers: two photocopies, a legal pad, and her laptop with forty-one browser tabs open. The prompt on the whiteboard, in the advisor's tidy hand, read "Compare two scholarly articles on the same question." Forty-one tabs, and she had found exactly one article worth comparing.

"Still hunting for the second one?" Marisol dropped into the chair across from her and peeled the foil off a protein bar. The club was small enough that everyone knew everyone's project, which was either the point or the problem, depending on the week.

"Every single paper I find says the same thing," Ava said. "That mindfulness training lowers test anxiety. Every one. I've been through the databases twice. I thought scholarship was supposed to be an argument." She turned the legal pad toward Marisol, who leaned over the columns of citations, all of them helpfully circling the same conclusion, like wagons.

"It's kind of convenient," Marisol said, mouth half full. "For your paper, I mean. You could just agree with everything."

That was precisely what bothered her, though Ava didn't say so yet. She had learned, in a statistics unit the previous spring, a phrase she'd written on the inside cover of her notebook and then half forgotten. The class had been stuffy, late afternoon, the teacher rushing to finish before the bell. Someone asked why the textbook made effects sound so reliable, and the teacher had tossed out a name for the trouble almost in passing, a name Ava now couldn't retrieve, only the shape of it, something domestic, something about storage.

By the time the others arrived, Theo with his coffee and Priya with her half-finished story about a lighthouse keeper, Ava had stopped pretending to take notes on the first article. She was typing search terms instead, chasing the phrase. It surfaced on the fourth try, and when it did she sat back so quickly that her chair scraped.

"File drawer problem," she said aloud. The others looked up. "Robert Rosenthal, 1979. Studies with null results go unpublished, so the published record looks more positive than the evidence." She read it off the screen almost verbatim, then looked around the table, the idea rearranging her forty-one tabs in her mind. The studies finding nothing, the ones that would have complicated her tidy columns, might be sitting in drawers somewhere, invisible.

"That's the second article," Priya said slowly. "Or, the missing second article. That's your review."

"No," Theo said. "You can't review what doesn't exist." He said it reasonably, the way he said most things, and Ava felt the problem tighten around her. He was right in one sense and wrong in another, and she couldn't yet say where the line fell. She copied the citation details of her one good article onto a fresh page, the way a lawyer prepares for a deposition, gathering what was known before testing what wasn't.

Here was the fact she had withheld even from Marisol, because it embarrassed her: three weeks earlier, before she understood any of this, she had emailed a psychology professor whose study she'd found dull, because it showed no effect, and asked, politely, whether he had published anything more definitive. He had never answered, and she had closed the tab with relief. Now she opened her sent folder and found the message still there, her own words looking younger than she remembered. The study showing no effect was real, had been conducted, had simply never made it into a journal. She typed a second email with her hands slightly unsteady, apologizing for the first, asking whether he could share it anyway.

She read the reply out loud when it came, twenty minutes into the meeting, while the others pretended not to wait for it. He would send it. He thanked her for asking, said it happened less often than it should. The attachment opened on her screen: dense, careful, null. Ava set the two documents side by side, the published and the unpublished, and began, for the first time that afternoon, to write.

"What's your thesis going to be?" Marisol asked, collecting wrappers from the table.

"I don't know yet," Ava said. "Something like: the honest comparison isn't between these two papers. It's between these two and everything I can't see." She pulled her chair closer to the table and started a new page.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Marxist historian Albert Soboul argued the Revolution was the moment the bourgeoisie overthrew feudal society and became the dominant class.
story:
The library smelled of warm dust and the lemon polish the custodian worked into the tables on Fridays, and by three o'clock the light through the tall windows had gone the color of weak tea. Angelina spread her books across the carrel in a fan: Carlyle, Tocqueville, a fat blue anthology of revolutionary historiography, and, at the center, her notebook open to a page titled, in handwriting that had already begun confidently and then shrunk, "Views since 1800." Below the title were two lines only, crossed out. The assignment was due in nine days. She had understood, vaguely, that historians disagreed about the French Revolution, but she had not understood that the disagreement itself was the subject, that she was being asked to map the arguments rather than adjudicate them, and the size of this misunderstanding had been sitting in her chest since Monday like a swallowed stone.

At the museum last weekend she had stood in front of a wall panel about 1789, reading the label while her little brother complained about wanting the café. The label called it a bourgeois revolution, plain and untroubled, as if that were simply what it was called. She had read the phrase twice and felt an odd friction, a sense that some particular person must have decided on those words, some person with a name and a desk, and that the label was quoting that person without saying so. She had taken a photo of it on her phone. It was still there, the white text and the small engraving of the Bastille behind it, and now, in the library, she set the phone beside the notebook and looked between them.

Her friend Priya arrived at four with a paper cup of tea and no apologies for being late. She dropped into the opposite chair and peered at the fanned books. "You've been here since lunch," she said. "Your hair's doing the thing."

"I'm trying to figure out whose idea that is," Angelina said, and turned the phone toward her. "The bourgeois thing. It's on the museum wall like it's the weather. Somebody wrote that."

Priya squinted at the photo. "Isn't it just what everyone says? Bourgeois revolution, middle class, the whole thing."

"That's what I want to know. Whether it's everyone or someone." Angelina pulled the blue anthology toward her and ran her finger down the table of contents until she found the chapter on Marxist interpretation. The author was Albert Soboul. She read the opening page quickly, then again, slowly, and the room seemed to sharpen around her, the radiator's tick and the far-off clatter of a book cart both suddenly distinct.

She looked up. "Okay. Here. Albert Soboul, the Marxist historian. He argued the Revolution was the moment the bourgeoisie overthrew feudal society and became the dominant class. That's the label. That's whose interpretation it is. The museum is quoting a dead French Marxist and not telling anybody."

"So it's wrong?"

Angelina shook her head, and then, honest even with herself in the privacy of her own skull, shook it again more slowly. "No. It's a position. There's a difference between a fact and a position that I don't think I knew there was, before this week." She had, in fact, been something of a neophyte about it, treating every textbook sentence as if it descended from the sky, and the discovery that sentences had authors with allegiances had transfigured the whole shelf of books in front of her, so that she now read the spines the way she would read a row of faces.

Priya sipped her tea. "But somebody must be right. Either the middle class took over or it didn't."

"That's what Carlyle thought, sort of, except he thought it was all a tragedy of mob violence, and Tocqueville thought the Revolution just continued something the monarchy started. And then there are people after Soboul who say the whole class-conflict story is too neat." Angelina tapped the notebook. "So my essay can't be 'what happened.' It has to be 'what people said happened, and when, and what they were looking at when they said it.'"

Priya made a small petulant sound, the sound of a student who had expected history to be memorizable and was being told it was an argument. "That's so much worse."

"It's so much better," Angelina said, though she said it quietly, testing it. Because she was not entirely sure. Somewhere under the thrill of the discovery was an uneasiness: if every account came from somewhere, from a politics or a decade or a grudge, then what was she supposed to stand on? She could line up the interpretations like evidence in a case, but the case might not have a verdict, and a part of her still wanted one, wanted the clean reward of a right answer the way she had wanted it all through school.

She picked up her pen and, instead of a thesis, wrote a question at the top of the fresh page: "Who called it bourgeois, and who stopped?" Underneath she began to list, in columns, Carlyle's grief, Tocqueville's continuity, Soboul's class ascendency, and the revisionists whose names she would need to check out on Thursday. The list was crooked and she did not straighten it. Outside the tall windows a groundskeeper was pushing a mower across the quad in long, patient lines, and Angelina watched him reach the far hedge, turn, and start back.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In her 2017 book 'Radical Candor', Kim Scott argues good feedback combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly.
story:
Charles sat through the first course of his sister's engagement dinner with his phone warm in his pocket, a draft message to Marcus still unsent. Marcus had anchored their robotics project to his own gearbox design for six weeks, and the gearbox kept slipping under load, and Charles, who was the one running the test rig, had written "looks off, maybe check it?" in the team chat and left it there. They had lost the regional qualifier on Saturday by a margin anyone could trace back to that slip. His aunt was telling a story about the caterer, his grandmother was correcting the details, and Charles was thinking about how "maybe check it" had cost them the season.

"You're somewhere else," his sister Dana said, leaning down the table past the candle his mother had lit even though it was only five o'clock. "You've cut your lamb into a grid. Like a censor cutting up a letter."

"Sorry. Team stuff."

"Since when does team stuff follow you to my dinner?"

"Since we lost." He put down his fork. "It's my fault, kind of. I knew Marcus's gearbox was failing and I didn't say anything real about it. I said it in a way he could ignore."

His cousin Priya, home from her first term at McGill, looked up from across the table. "My roommate did a whole presentation on this. There's a book. Kim Scott, 2017. She says good feedback has to do both things at once: you actually care about the person, and you challenge them directly. Skip either half and it stops working."

"What's it called?" Charles asked.

"Radical candor," Priya said, and went back to dismantling a dinner roll.

Charles turned his water glass a quarter turn on the tablecloth. He had assumed, without ever examining the assumption, that kindness and directness were opposites, that every honest sentence took something out of the friendship it was aimed at. And he had also assumed, on other days, that being blunt was a form of respect, that Marcus would eventually thank him for a flat "your design is wrong." Both positions had a certain contrivance to them now that he held them up against Priya's sentence. Each one had let him feel principled while doing nothing.

"Say it worked," he said. "Say I'd told him in October. Specific. 'The gearbox slips when the load goes past four kilograms, here's the data.' What's that cost me?"

"Nothing," Dana said. "You'd have been doing your job."

"It might have cost me him." He thought of Marcus in the lab at eleven at night, teaching the freshmen how to solder, remembering everyone's coffee order, staying after regionals to pack the trailer while everyone else went for pizza. A person like that, Charles could have hurt without meaning to, with a sentence shaped wrong. "He'd have taken 'your design is wrong' as 'you are wrong.' He doesn't split those."

"So split them for him," Priya said. "Say the design, not the person, and say it with data, and say it because you want him to succeed. That's the whole thing. The caring isn't a wrapper you put on the criticism. It's half the criticism."

Their grandfather asked from the head of the table what a gearbox was, and for a few minutes the conversation belonged to him, and Charles's mother refilled glasses, and the dinner went on around him the way family dinners do, interminable and warm and full of people finishing each other's sentences. He let it carry him. Under the noise he was assembling the message. Not an apology, or not only. An account of what he had seen, when he had seen it, and what he had failed to do with it, followed by the thing he should have said in October, said now in October's plain vocabulary: the slip, the load, the numbers, the fix he thought was possible, and a line offering to run the tests with him over break.

There was a part he still could not resolve, and he was honest enough with himself to sit with it rather than paper over it. Even feedback that was specific and kind had to be received, and Marcus had spent six weeks believing in the gearbox, and belief did not always go quietly. Priya's book, whatever else was in it, couldn't guarantee that. Charles could control the shape of the sentence, not the room the sentence landed in. He decided that this was not a reason to stay silent; it was only a risk, and risks of that kind were the tax on being useful to someone. He might be wrong about that too. He would find out.

Between the main course and the cake, he stepped out to the hallway where the coats were, and typed the message with both thumbs, and read it once, and cut the phrase "I should have said this sooner" because it was about Charles rather than about the gearbox, and left the numbers in, and sent it. Then he stood for a while with his forehead near the cold window, watching his uncle arrive late and park badly, one wheel up on the curb.

When he came back to the table his phone buzzed in his pocket. He kept his hands on the tablecloth, on either side of the dessert plate, through his grandmother's toast, through Dana's laugh at the end of it, through the candle guttering in its own wax. Only when the plates were being stacked did he look. It was Marcus: "four kg? run it tuesday. bring the rig." Charles wrote back, "Tuesday. I'll bring donuts too," and pocketed the phone, and reached for the stack of plates in front of his grandfather, and started carrying them to the kitchen.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Each transfer RNA carries one amino acid and has a three-base anticodon that pairs with the matching codon on the messenger RNA.
story:
Sadie got to the community garden ten minutes early and laid the index cards out on the bench in rows, because if Mr. Okafor thought she couldn't handle translation, she was going to prove him wrong in front of everyone. The cards had come out of her own pocket, twenty of them, each one labeled with three letters on one side and an amino acid name on the other. She had written them at midnight with a felt pen that bled through the paper.

"They're turgid," Dev said, dropping onto the bench beside her and picking one up. He meant the tomato seedlings in the bed behind them, their leaves gone soft and folded after yesterday's heat, but he looked at her cards too, flipping AUG between his fingers. "You didn't have to make these."

"I wanted to." She took the card back. That wasn't the whole truth. She wanted to be the one holding the cards, the one others had to come to, because on the last quiz she'd written that ribosomes made proteins out of DNA directly and Mr. Okafor had read it aloud, gently, which was worse than if he'd laughed.

The rest of the class filed in through the gate with the fake grass strip Mr. Okafor called the messenger RNA. It was a long paper ribbon with codons printed every few inches, and two students held it taut between the bean trellises. Sadie watched Marcus and Priya take the ends and felt her stomach tighten, because holding the ribbon was a job with no thinking in it, and she hadn't been assigned it, which meant she'd been assigned something harder.

"Sadie, you're a transfer RNA," Mr. Okafor said, and walked away before she could ask anything, which was his method and she hated it.

She stood at the start of the ribbon with her card, AUG facing out, amino acid name methionine pressed against her palm. Marcus read the first codon printed on the paper. "AUG," he said. Sadie looked at her card, then at the ribbon, then stepped forward and pressed her card to the paper so the three letters met the three letters.

"It matches," Priya said. "So you can hand over your amino acid."

Sadie did, passing the methionine card to Elias, who was playing the growing protein chain and stood there holding it like a live coal. Then she went to the back of the line for another card and got one that said GGU, arginine. She walked the ribbon until she found GCC, pressed the card against it, and handed Elias the arginine. Three bases on her side, three bases printed on the ribbon, and they met.

"It's like a lock," she said.

"Everyone says that," Dev said. He had a card with no match anywhere on the ribbon and was loitering near the compost bin, sulking. "It's a lock, it's a code, it's a recipe. Pick your metaphor and stop pretending it's knowledge."

"It's not a metaphor if it's literally three letters matching three letters." She held up her card. "I carry one amino acid. One. And this three-letter thing on me pairs with the three-letter thing on the messenger RNA. That's the whole job."

"Then why does it exist?" Dev said. "Somebody had to design the matching."

"Nobody had to." She heard her own voice get flat and stopped. This was the argument she'd had with him since sixth grade, his habit of finding a purpose behind everything, her refusal to. "It's not working toward anything. It's just chemistry that happens to copy itself."

"So you say." He shrugged and didn't give the card back when she reached for it.

Mr. Okafor drifted over. "Dev, does your card match anything?"

"Not yet."

"Then you're standing in the wrong place. Walk." Dev walked, sulk intact, and found his match near the trellis, three letters against three letters, no purpose required. He didn't say anything about it, and Sadie didn't point it out, because she knew how it felt to be wrong in front of people.

She kept working the ribbon. One card at a time, one amino acid handed to Elias, whose chain of cards was getting long enough that he had to hold it against his chest. Somewhere near the middle she found a codon where her card almost matched, two letters agreeing and the third not, and she stood there for a long moment with her thumb over the mismatched base, wanting it to fit.

"You could just pretend," Priya offered.

Sadie put the card down and went to the back of the line. "Then the protein would be wrong." She wasn't sure that was exactly true, whether one wrong letter meant a wrong protein or sometimes meant nothing at all, and she decided she'd look it up tonight instead of guessing out loud.

By the end of the period Elias held a chain of eleven cards and read the names off like a roll call. "Methionine, arginine, leucine, valine..."

"Stop," Dev said suddenly. "That's not a protein. That's a list."

"It's both," Sadie said, and picked her cards up off the bench, one by one, and squared them against her palm.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: By specializing and trading, two countries can each end up consuming combinations of goods that lie beyond what they could produce on their own.
story:
The assignment was due Monday, and Jacob had brought it to work folded in his back pocket, because Tuesday was the midterm and he could not afford another C. The graph showed two countries, one that could make a lot of fish and a little wheat, one that could make a lot of wheat and not much fish. He had drawn their production possibility curves, the smooth arcs his textbook loved, and then the practice problem told him to mark the point each country ended up at after trading. He had plotted it, and it sat outside the curve. He stared at it on his break in the stockroom, where the smell of cardboard and cold pineapple clung to everything, and thought he had made an arithmetic error. He checked it twice. The point stayed stubbornly beyond the line he had drawn, in the empty white space where his professor had written "unattainable" in the notes.

He was still frowning at it when Dani pushed through the plastic flaps with a cart of dented cans. "You look like a person doing taxes for fun."

"Econ," Jacob said. "Look at this. Country A can produce anywhere on this curve, right? Fish, wheat, any mix along the line. But after they trade, the problem says they end up here." He tapped the dot. "That's outside. That's not something they can make."

Dani set a can of chickpeas on the shelf and leaned over his notebook. She was a sophomore at the community college, and she had opinions about everything, and usually they were loud. "Maybe the book's wrong."

"The book's not wrong. There's a whole section on it." He flipped pages. The section had a name, comparative advantage, and paragraphs of jargon that slid off him like water off the waxed floor of aisle six. "It keeps saying both countries gain. Both. Even if one of them is better at making both things, they both gain. That's the part that sounds like a lie."

"It does sound like a lie," Dani agreed. "My uncle says trade is how this country gets robbed. He calls it a plot by the plutocracy, the rich people who run everything, deciding what gets made where so the rest of us eat the cost." She stacked another can. "He's not completely wrong about the rich people part."

Jacob had an uncle like that too, a man who maligne every trade deal by name, blamed each one for the closed mill and the empty storefronts on Route 9, and was right about some of it, Jacob suspected, and wrong about the rest. That was what kept snagging him. He wanted to hold both things at once: the town that lost the mill, and this dot sitting calmly outside a curve it had no business sitting outside of.

"Okay," he said slowly. "Wait." He pulled the pen from behind his ear. "Here's what it doesn't say. It doesn't say they produce at that point. The dot isn't what they make. It's what they get to have. Consume, or whatever. They still make stuff on their own curve, but if each one makes mostly the thing it's least bad at giving up, and then they swap, then after the swap each country can end up with a combination of fish and wheat that's beyond anything it could have produced by itself." He looked up. "That's the whole trick. The line is what you can make. The trade point is what you can have. Two different things."

Dani squinted at the graph. "So the country that's worse at everything still wins?"

"Still gains. Not the same as winning. It can still be a poor country." He was honest about that much, because the textbook was not. The graph said nothing about who kept the surplus, and he suspected that was where his uncle's anger lived, in the space the graph left blank. The math was clean and the world was not, and he could not yet tell how much of the messiness the math was hiding and how much it genuinely solved.

"Whatever," Dani said, checking her phone. "If it gets you a B, trade away." She shoved the cart toward the flaps, then stopped, half in and half out of the stockroom's fluorescent light. "Show me the dot thing again Tuesday, if it works. I might take that class." The flaps swung shut behind her, breathing out cold air and the green smell of the produce aisle. Jacob looked down at the point outside the curve, the small penciled X that had no right to be there and was there anyway, and traced over it once, dark and sure.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Near Earth's surface a projectile's vertical velocity changes by about 9.8 metres per second every second, whether it is rising or falling.
story:
The launcher stood in the corner of the physics gallery, a brass tube on a pivoting base with two dials, one for angle and one for launch speed, and a foam target hung twelve metres away on the far wall. Hailey had already missed it four times. The fifth ball arced high, smacked the wall a metre above the target, and rolled back to her feet like a reproach. Her lab partner, Jules, stood beside the exhibit with his phone out, filming each failure, which was supposed to be for their project and felt more like evidence for the prosecution.

"I need this," Hailey said. She picked up the ball. "My grade needs this."

"Your grade needs you to stop aiming like it's a basketball." Jules lowered the phone. "You keep watching the target and pulling the dial toward it. That's not math, that's hope."

She had come to the museum because Ms. Ferreira had handed back the projectile quiz with a single line at the top, and because her mother had threatened, not for the first time, to lambaste the school's entire science department for Hailey's incipient collapse in a subject she had once loved. The retake was Monday. It was Saturday. She had two days and a museum and a boy who owed her a favor after she'd covered his shift at the library.

Her little brother, Marcus, had tried to help the night before, in the backyard with a stopwatch and a tennis ball. He'd thrown straight up and timed the flight while she called out the numbers, and she had written them all down, and one of them had stopped her cold. The ball had taken just as long coming down as it had going up. She had stared at the paper and said, "That can't be right, it slows down going up, it should crawl at the top." Marcus had only shrugged and thrown the ball again, higher, and the stopwatch had said the same thing.

Now she crouched at the launcher with her notebook open on the floor, the backyard numbers at the top of the page. "Okay. Say it out loud with me," she said. "The vertical velocity changes by 9.8 metres per second every second. Going up and coming down, same rate."

"Which means what?" Jules asked, not cruelly, but not kindly either.

"It means the up part and the down part are symmetric. It's rising, it's slowing, it stops for an instant, and then it falls, speeding up at the same rate it slowed down. Nine point eight every second, whether it's rising or falling." She tapped the page. "And the sideways part, the horizontal, none of that applies. Sideways it just goes at whatever speed it left with."

"So you're saying they're separate."

"I'm saying they're separate." She heard herself say it and felt the shape of the thing she'd been missing all week, the way she'd been treating the ball's path as one motion, one judgment, one arc to eyeball. It wasn't. It was two clean straight lines of reasoning laid over each other, and only one of them was complicated. She thought of her father, who fixed engines by refusing to look at the whole car, who isolated one system at a time, and of Ms. Ferreira's opposite creed, that everything in physics was one connected fabric. Both were true, she decided, if you knew when to hold each view. She also knew, and was honest enough to admit to the notebook if not to Jules, that she couldn't yet have said exactly when.
