She set the angle to thirty degrees, did the arithmetic in the margin twice, divided the launch speed into a vertical piece and a horizontal piece, counted how long the vertical piece would last before it came back down, and multiplied the horizontal piece by that time. Twelve metres. She turned the speed dial to the number she'd gotten and stepped back.

The ball left the tube, rose, hung, fell, and struck the target dead center with a sound like a knuckle rapped on a door. The exhibit chimed. Somewhere behind her a small boy clapped.

Jules looked at his phone, then at her, then at the phone again. "Do that again," he said.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Under US law, an artwork is protected by copyright automatically the moment it is created in a fixed form; registration is voluntary, though needed before suing over a US work.
story:
The printmaking studio at Camp Merrow smelled of ink and vinegar, and by the second week Alexia had stopped noticing it. She had noticed other things instead: the way her counselor's clipboard listed every camper's portfolio deadline in red, and the fact that hers was still blank. Ten artworks, one theme, one artist's statement, due on the last Friday. Everyone else had chosen something by now. Priya was doing doors. Marcus was doing his grandmother's hands. Alexia had made four pieces in two days and hated all four, and on Tuesday she carried the worst of them to the picnic table behind the boathouse and laid it out flat, the way you might lay out evidence.

"Is that supposed to be a river?" Priya sat down across from her with a peanut butter sandwich.

"It's supposed to be a flood. I was going to do water."

"You already told me water feels like everyone's theme."

"That's the problem. Everything I think of either feels like mine for about an hour or like it belongs to a genealogy of other people's work that goes back forever." Alexia turned the print so Priya could see it right side up. "This is the fourth thing I've ruined."

Priya looked at it for a while, chewing. The lake behind them made its small, patient sounds. "It looks like something that used to be a river," she said finally. "Like after. Like what's left when the thing is over."

Alexia looked again. In the print the water had gone thin and gray where she had overworked the plate, and what remained were the objects the water had left behind, a fence post, a shoe, the silhouette of a house roof. The accident had made the picture into what was left afterward. She turned it back around so she couldn't keep staring at it, because she could feel herself starting to want it, and wanting something you made by accident was dangerous.

The theme arrived the next morning anyway, in the way themes do, wearing someone else's crisis. They were in the computer lab to scan their work for the camp's online gallery, and Marcus was standing at the far terminal with his arms crossed, refusing to press upload. "Once it's out there, it's out there," he was saying to no one in particular. "Anyone can just take it. Use it for whatever."

"You could watermark them," someone offered.

"That doesn't stop anyone either."

Alexia was about to say something dismissive when she realized she didn't actually know, and the not knowing bothered her more than Marcus's drama. That evening she sat on her bunk with the camp's sad laptop and looked it up, expecting to find a maze of forms and fees. Instead the first result said it plainly. Your artwork is protected automatically, the moment you create it in a fixed form. You don't have to do anything. Registration is voluntary. She read it twice, then kept reading down the page, and stopped at one more line: you do need to register before you can sue over a US work. She read that twice as well, because it changed the shape of the first part without canceling it.

"Did you know," she said to Priya at breakfast, "that the second you make something, it's already protected? Copyright. Automatically. You don't have to register or anything."

"Then why is Marcus having a breakdown?"

"Registration is voluntary," Alexia said, "but if you actually want to sue somebody over a US work, you have to have done it first." She spread jam on her toast. "So you're protected, but the protection is kind of like my river. It's there. What you can do with it is the part that's left after."

Priya considered this. "That's a trenchant toast observation."

"It's a theme observation." Alexia set down her knife. "What's left after. The flood is the making. The portfolio is what's left."

The rest of the week became the busiest of her summer. She stopped trying to invent and started collecting aftermaths: the print of the drained river, a charcoal drawing of the studio sink at night with its coagulated ink rag drying on the rim, a photograph of the fire circle on Sunday morning after Saturday night, ash and a folding chair someone had left tilted. She kept Marcus's worry taped inside her sketchbook, not as a joke but as a second way of seeing the same thing. He thought putting work online meant losing it. She thought everything made was already a kind of loss, paint leaving the brush, the moment becoming the object, and that the object was still hers anyway, protected the instant it existed in any fixed form, which was its own quiet consolation. She could not fully reconcile the two views. She decided the portfolio could hold both.

On Thursday, Marcus found her at the picnic table, sorting prints into the order she wanted for the statement. He stood with his hands in his pockets. "Someone told me you looked up the copyright thing," he said. "For me."

"It's automatic. The moment it's fixed. You could post your grandmother's hands and they'd still be yours."

"Yours too, right? Yours would be yours."

"Mine are mine," she said. "Although technically if I ever wanted to sue someone over them, I'd have to register first. That part's voluntary until it isn't." She smoothed the corner of the drained river print. "Which is basically my whole statement, if you want to know the ending before the opening."

Marcus sat down and picked up the photograph of the fire circle. He turned it over, then back. "I want to trade," he said. "One of my hands drawings for the print Priya said was an accident. The river one."

"You want the accident."

"The accident and the whole story that goes with it," he said, and reached across the table for it before she could answer.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: In Chicago, MLA and APA styles, entries in the final list of sources are arranged alphabetically by the author's surname, not in the order the sources were cited.
story:
The library's third floor smelled like radiator dust and old laminate, and Hannah had claimed the corner table by the window since before the first bell. Her research paper was due in nine days, and in front of her sat two stacks: one of notecards, soft at the edges from being shuffled, and one of photocopied pages, each flagged with a pink sticker in the order she had used it. Her thesis was underlined twice at the top of her outline: that the city's decision to close the public pools had been less about budget than about who the pools belonged to. She had twelve sources and a bibliography that ran a page and a half, and she was almost done.

Almost done, until Marcus dropped his bag on the chair across from her and pulled her paper toward him without asking. They had been assigned as writing partners in September, a pairing Hannah had resented at first, then tolerated, and now, in February, relied on in a way she never said out loud. He read fast, his finger moving down the left margin, and stopped at the last page.

"Your works cited is wrong," he said.

"It's not wrong. Every source is there."

"Look at the order." He turned the paper so it faced her. "First entry is the city council minutes. Then that newspaper thing from 1974. Then the interview with the lifeguard."

"That's the order I used them in," Hannah said. "That's how I found them."

Marcus leaned back. "It doesn't go by the order you used them."

She put her hand flat over the page, which was a gesture she'd learned from her mother, who did it with bills. "Then what does it go by?"

"In MLA, and Chicago, and APA too, the final list is alphabetical by the author's last name. Not by when you cited them." He said it plainly, the way he said most things, and slid the paper back to her. "So your lifeguard, Alvarez, goes first. Your council minutes are under C."

Hannah looked at the list and felt the whole careful architecture of her afternoon shift. She had built the bibliography like a diary, one entry for each step of her discovery, and now it had to be rebuilt like a phone book. "Nobody told me that."

"It's in the handbook," Marcus said. "Page eleven. There's a whole section on it."

She remembered then the night in October when she had stayed up until two reordering her chemistry lab by the temperature readings instead of the trial numbers, certain she was right, and Mr. Okafor had handed it back with a single red circle and no comment. She had cried in the stairwell, briefly, and told no one. The memory arrived now with a familiar heat behind it, and she pushed her chair back from the table so hard it banged the radiator.

"Don't do the sigh," Marcus said.

"I didn't sigh."

"You did the thing before the sigh." He was already pulling the handbook from her bag, where he knew it was, because he had watched her wedge it in that morning. He opened it and set it beside her bibliography, side by side, and waited. That was their arrangement, unspoken and enforced by both of them: he would find the problem, she would fix it, and neither would pretend the moment was pleasant.

Hannah picked up her pen. She started a fresh page and wrote Alvarez at the top, then Bloomquist, whose florid op-ed about "the sacred institution of the municipal pool" she had quoted twice and now suspected she'd have to cut. As she worked, copying entries and reordering them, she found herself slowing down at the council minutes. In her first draft, they had appeared third, after the newspaper had framed the story and before the interview had humanized it. Her argument had been built in that sequence, deliberately, the way a person walks into a room. Alphabetical, the minutes came second, and something about her essay's middle section felt suddenly exposed, as if the evidence had walked in ahead of her thesis.

"Marcus. If I reorder the list, do I have to reorder the paper?"

He looked up from his own draft. "The citations in the text stay wherever you said them. Only the list at the end changes."

"That's not what I mean." She heard her own voice go clipped and did not soften it. "I mean the way I argued it. I set it up so the reader gets the newspaper first, because the newspaper makes the closure sound boring. Then the minutes show it wasn't. If everything's alphabetical, doesn't the paper itself sort of adumbrate its own ending? Like the reader could just skip to the list and see what's coming?"

Marcus considered this longer than he usually considered anything. "Nobody reads the bibliography first."

"I might."

They had reached the edge of an old argument, the one about whether a paper was a case being argued or a record being kept, and Hannah felt the familiar tension gather, the one that usually ended with one of them packing up early. Instead she picked up her pen again and wrote two columns on the back of a notecard: one headed ARGUE, one headed RECORD. Under ARGUE she put the order she had written. Under RECORD she wrote the alphabet, all the way down to Vasquez, and looked between them.

"I can do both," she said slowly. "Keep the essay in my order. Alphabetize the list. But I don't know which one the essay actually is." She turned the notecard over, then back. "That part I can't footnote."

Marcus pulled his chair around to her side of the table and picked up the Vasquez entry, squinting at it. "You spelled this one wrong," he said. "There's no h."

Hannah took the card from him and looked at it for a long moment.

"Get me the white-out," she said.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: A getter that returns a reference to a private mutable object, such as a list, lets outside code change it, so programmers often return a copy instead.
story:
The coding club met in the back corner of the library, four tables pushed together under a skylight that made everyone's screens glare at four o'clock. Maika arrived early to claim the seat by the outlet, because her laptop held its charge the way a sieve held water. She was on her third attempt at the Java assignment: a class called Playlist with a private ArrayList of songs, a method to add a song, a getter, and a test class to prove it all worked. The plan looked elegant on paper. The compiler had opinions.

"Yours is throwing that too?" Desh asked, leaning over. He had an empty screen and a full coffee, which was his usual ratio. Desh wanted, more than anything, to monetize the little study app he'd built for the club, and he treated every assignment as a rehearsal for that. "Private fields, getters, the whole ritual. Mr. Okafor grades hard on structure."

"I know how to write the getter," Maika said, then caught herself, because she didn't like how it sounded, like she was brushing him off. She turned the laptop so he could see. "Look, I'm stuck on the test. Watch."

She ran it. The test created a Playlist, added three songs, called the getter, and printed the list. Then, in the test class itself, she called the getter again and used it to clear the list. She printed the playlist one more time through its own toString method. The first print showed three songs. The second showed an empty pair of brackets.

"That's wrong," Desh said. "The field's private. That's the whole point of private. Nothing outside should be able to touch it."

Maika put her pen down. She had a habit of arguing both sides of a question before she'd finished losing the first one, and she could feel it starting now. "But the getter works," she said. "It gave the test code the list, and the test code cleared it. So either private is a lie, or the getter gave it something more than a look." She scrolled up to the getter, a single line that returned the field directly, and stared at it the way you stare at a door you left open.

Priya slid into the seat across from them, fifteen minutes late and unbothered about it, holding a paper cup of noodles she wasn't supposed to have in the library. Priya's want for the semester was simpler and louder than anyone else's: she was determined to be the first person in the club to finish the whole unit test suite, so she could put it in the club's shared folder with her name at the top. She was not, as Desh had once said in her hearing, a sycophant about it; she just liked winning, and she liked it openly.

"Maika's playlist deleted itself," Desh told her.

"Nothing deletes itself," Priya said, and slurped her noodles. "Show me."

Maika ran the test again, and Priya watched the empty brackets appear a second time with the expression of someone watching a magic trick she intended to catch. "Do it again but return a copy," she said. "In the getter. Copy the list and return the copy. If the test still empties the playlist, I'll eat this without a fork."

"You just want to see me write more code," Maika said, but she was already typing. She made the getter build a new ArrayList from the private one and return that instead, then ran the test. The test code cleared the copy it had received. The playlist, printing itself through its own method, still showed all three songs. Maika sat back. Outside code could empty what it held, but the private field stayed full, and she understood, in one clean moment, that the getter had been handing out the actual list before, not a picture of it. Returning a copy fixed it because the copy was what outside code got to hold.

"Sanguine about your grade now?" Desh asked.

"Halfway," Maika said. She highlighted the two versions of the getter and saved them both in a file she called evidence.txt. "Here's what I can't decide. The copy costs something every time you call it, right, you're building a new list each time. So when is that worth it? If nobody's going to mutate the list, the plain return is faster and the copy is a tax." She looked at Priya, then at Desh. "I believe the copy is safer. I don't know that it's always better. I'm not going to pretend those are the same thing."

Priya had already copied Maika's test into her own project, and her hand was hovering over the shared folder, ready to upload it with her name in the header. She paused, cursor blinking, and looked at the two getters side by side on Maika's screen. Then she deleted her name from the comment and typed Maika's instead.

"First finish still counts," Priya said. "I'm just finishing it honestly." She hit upload, and the little progress bar crept across the screen while Desh, behind them, quietly opened his study app and started changing every getter he'd ever written.

"Maika," he said. "How many of these do you think I have to fix before Friday?"

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: With typical use, about 13 in 100 people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy, mostly because condoms are not used correctly every time.
story:
The waiting room had four chairs, three of them taken, and Tyler took the fourth with the folded paper pressed flat under his thigh so he would not keep rereading it. The paper was his script. In forty minutes, in the conference room down the hall, he was supposed to run his first session as a peer health educator for the summer program at the clinic, and the whole thing had come together only because Dr. Okafor had said, back in May, "You talk to people. That's rarer than you think." He had wanted to believe her. Then yesterday his younger brother, Marcus, sixteen and armored in certainty, had stood in their kitchen and said the sessions were a waste of time, that everybody already knew everything, and something about the way he said it had catalyzed Tyler's own doubt into a real and specific fear: that he would stand up there and know nothing the room wanted.

"Tyler Reyes," the nurse called, and he followed her back to a small office where Dr. Okafor sat behind a desk stacked with pamphlet boxes. "You're early," she said. "Good. Let's hear it."

He ran through what he had. Consent first, because the training manual put it first: a yes that is freely given, that can change, that has to be there every time and not just once. He made himself say it out loud to her, plainly, without the hedge words he had written and crossed out and rewritten on the bus. Then contraception, and then how the clinic did testing for infections, walk-in hours on Tuesdays, results in under a week, nobody billed without asking first. Dr. Okafor nodded along and did not correct him, which felt like a kind of weather.

It was the condoms he stumbled on. He had a fact on his paper, circled twice, and he still half believed it could not be right. "With typical use," he said, "about thirteen in a hundred people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy." He looked up. "Thirteen. The box makes them sound basically perfect."

Dr. Okafor did not explain it, which was her way. She only said, "So what do you do with that number?"

He sat with it. In health class last spring a girl near the window had said almost the same thing, had actually laughed, called the statistic broken, and the teacher had moved on. Tyler had moved on too. Now he turned the number over and found the two ideas he had been carrying without noticing they were rivals. One said the number proved condoms were bad, that the whole business was a lie sold in foil wrappers; that was the version Marcus would like, and it had the shape of an argument an ideologue would admire, one clean conclusion from one clean fact. The other idea said the number was a reason for despair dressed up as realism, the ascetic answer, that nothing worked so nothing was worth doing carefully. He had believed both at different moments on the bus.

"Neither," he said slowly. "It's not that they fail. It's how people actually use them, real people, tired people, people in a hurry." Dr. Okafor raised an eyebrow at the edge of an explanation he should not give, since the training had been firm about staying inside what the fact said. He pulled back. "I mean, what I can say is the number itself. Thirteen in a hundred with typical use, over a year, for people relying only on condoms. I can say that out loud and let it be true, and then say what lowers the risk, and where to get tested, and that it's free on Tuesdays." He heard how it sounded, unglamorous, like giving directions. It also sounded like something a person could actually use.

"Say the hard part," she said. "The part where somebody disagrees."

"Marcus thinks it's all obvious." He told her about the kitchen, the folded arms, the certainty. "And my mom thinks sixteen is too young for any of it, so he's getting it from guys at school, and they're getting it from the internet."

"So he'll be your hardest room," she said, "and your most important one, and you don't get to skip either one." She slid a box of pamphlets across the desk and stood. "Conference room's open. Put those on the front table and start on time even if nobody's there."

Five kids came, then a sixth, a girl with wet hair who took the chair nearest the door as if she might need it. Tyler set out the pamphlets, wrote Tuesdays, free, walk-in on the whiteboard, and began the way he had practiced, with consent, in his own words, no script. When he got to the condom statistic he said the number straight and then stopped talking, because the boy in the gray hoodie was already objecting, exactly as the girl in health class had, that the number had to be wrong.

"Thirteen out of a hundred," Tyler said again, and held the kid's eyes. "Typical use, one year, only condoms. That's the real number, not the one on the box." He let it sit. "So the honest question isn't whether it works. It's what you do knowing that, and who you ask when you want to know more." The girl by the door, the sixth one, raised her hand, and when he called on her she asked, quietly, whether the Tuesday testing needed a parent's signature. He said no. She wrote something on her palm, in blue ink, careful small letters, and did not leave early.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In Kahlo's The Broken Column (1944), her spine is painted as a cracked Ionic column visible through an opening in her body.
story:
The print of The Broken Column had been taped to the classroom door for a week before Julia let herself look at it properly. She had walked past it twice a day with her bag sliding off her shoulder, registering only a woman, a desert, some kind of wound. Now, on the Thursday before her presentation, she stood in the corridor with three minutes until the bell and understood that the thing showing through the opening in the woman's body was a column. An actual column, pale and classical, split down its length, holding up nothing.

"You're blocking the door," said Priya behind her, and Julia stepped aside without taking her eyes off the print.

"There's a Greek column inside her," Julia said. "Why is there a Greek column inside her?"

Priya leaned in, close enough that Julia could smell her cherry lip balm. "That's the spine," she said. "It's her spine. An Ionic one, see the scroll at the top, the capital." Priya tapped the glass with one knuckle. "My mum's an architect. Columns are basically all I know." The bell went off above them, and neither of them moved.

The assignment had seemed simple in September: choose a painting, write a formal analysis, present it to the class. Colour, composition, symbolism. Mr. Adeyemi had repeated the three words so often that Julia had begun to hear them as a kind of incantation, as though saying them in order would produce meaning on its own. She had picked Kahlo because the posters in her dentist's office had made the paintings look familiar, and familiar felt safe. Now she sat in the library during lunch with the print propped against a stack of geography textbooks, discovering that safety was the one thing the painting refused to offer. The sky was torn open by fissures the same pale grey as the column. The nails driven into the woman's skin echoed the fissures. Everything broken answered everything else broken, and the corset, white and clinical and strapped like a device for holding a body together, did not look like it was working.

She wrote "formal analysis" at the top of a page and then, underneath, the question that had actually been bothering her. Why a column? She could describe the composition in her sleep by now: the vertical figure centred, the horizontal seam of the corset cutting across it, the tears in the sky framing her like a broken halo. She could ascribe the tears to grief and the nails to pain and the corset to constraint, and Mr. Adeyemi would nod, and the class would clap politely, and none of it would be wrong. But it would also be the kind of answer you could give without looking at the painting at all, the kind assembled from the caption in the textbook, and something in her resisted giving it.

Priya found her there in the fourth lunch period, carrying two cartons of chips and a look of purpose. She set one carton in front of Julia without comment, which Julia understood to mean that Priya had noticed she hadn't eaten, and pulled up a chair. "My mum says Ionic columns are the ones with the scrolls," she said. "The clever-looking ones. The cerebral ones, she calls them, because they're slim and they hold up libraries and law courts." Priya salted her chips. "Yours is holding up a person."

Julia looked at the print again. "But it's cracked," she said slowly. "It's a cracked Ionic column, visible through an opening in her body. That's what the painting is. That's the whole thing. Her spine is a column and the column is broken." She heard how obvious it sounded and how strange it still was, both at once. "So when I say the corset symbolises constraint, I'm saying something the painting already says better. The corset is doing exactly what it looks like it's doing."

"So say that instead." Priya shrugged, as if this were nothing, but she had brought the chips, and she had come looking, and Julia felt the small weight of being looked after settle somewhere beneath her ribs.

The problem was that saying it instead meant admitting what she didn't know. On Friday night she tried to draft the presentation and kept stopping at the same place. She could argue that the column made the body into a building, a structure, something architectural that could fail architecturally. She could argue the opposite, that the column made the failure monumental, the way monuments are, and that Kahlo had painted her own damage as something classical, permanent, worth looking at with a kind of dignity. Both readings fit the painting. Both readings fit each other, even, in a way she couldn't yet articulate, and when she tried to choose one her draft went soft in the middle like a loaf pressed at its waist. She wrote a line about the grey of the sky matching the grey of the stone, crossed it out, wrote it again.

Mr. Adeyemi had told them, back in September, that the term before their class arrived had been a strange interregnum, a year without a proper art teacher, when the sixth formers taught themselves from a box of prints left in the cupboard. Julia thought about those students now, sitting in this same library with the same images and no one to ascribe anything to, and about Priya's mother passing on columns over a dinner table, and about how knowledge seemed to move sideways, hand to hand, more often than it dropped from above. She still didn't know which reading she would give the class. She knew only that she would give them both, and then stand there with the gap between them showing, the way the opening in the woman's body showed.

On Monday she carried the print to the front and clipped it to the easel. Twenty-six faces looked up at her, and Priya, third row, gave her a small nod that meant nothing to anyone else. "The first thing you see," Julia began, "is the opening in her body. And through the opening, her spine, painted as a cracked Ionic column." She let the class find it, watched their eyes travel to the pale scroll of the capital, the long split running down through the centre of her. "I'm going to tell you two things about it," she said, "and I don't think either one of them is wrong."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: White coat hypertension is when blood pressure reads high in a clinic, often from nervousness, but normal at home, so doctors may check it with home or all-day monitoring.
story:
The health aide training at Camp Wenonah ran for two weeks, and on the fourth day Nurse Reyes handed Alexandra a cuff and a stethoscope and told her to take Marcus's blood pressure. Marcus was a counselor from the waterfront, seventeen minutes from leading his afternoon swim block, and he sat on the cot in the infirmary with his knee bouncing. Alexandra wrapped the cuff above his elbow, found the pulse with two fingers, and pumped until the needle climbed past 160.

"Let me try the other arm," she said. The second reading was 158 over 96. She wrote both numbers on the card Reyes kept on the clipboard and stood there holding the clipboard the way you hold a test you already know you failed.

"That's high," Marcus said. He was not asking. His knee had not stopped bouncing since he sat down.

Reyes was across the room sorting gauze, and she did not come over. That was the arrangement for the whole training: Alexandra took the readings, Alexandra said what she thought, and Reyes corrected her afterward, in the debrief, never during. It was supposed to teach her to stand on her own feet. Mostly it taught her how long thirty seconds of silence could last.

"My dad's on pills for this," Marcus said. "He found out at a physical. One reading and the doctor started talking about medication." He looked at the numbers on the card again. "So that's it, then. I've got it too."

Alexandra had spent the previous evening in the infirmary's back room with the camp's one battered physiology text, learning what the two numbers were and how they moved. She knew that the top number was the pressure when the heart contracted and the bottom was the pressure between beats. She knew that regular aerobic exercise tended to bring both down over months, not days, and that a diet heavy in salt pushed them up while one built around vegetables, fruits, and less processed food pushed them down. She knew all of it in the quiet way you know things from a book, which is to say not yet in a way you can hand to a frightened person.

"Wait," she said. "Have you ever had it taken anywhere else? Like at the drugstore machine, or at home?"

"My mom has a cuff. She checks my dad sometimes. She did me once, like a year ago, and it was way lower than that."

Alexandra looked at the bouncing knee, at Marcus's hands folded too tightly in his lap, at the way he kept glancing at the door because his swim block started in twelve minutes. She thought about the drugstore machine, about his mother's cuff, about the difference between a number taken in a quiet kitchen and a number taken here, in a small room, by someone wearing a name tag, right before a doctor or a nurse might say something that changed your life.

"I don't think one reading in here means much," she said. "There's a thing called white coat hypertension. Some people's blood pressure reads high in a clinic just because they're nervous here, but it's normal when they take it at home. Doctors know about it. Before they draw any conclusion, they'll ask about home readings, or they'll have you do monitoring through a whole day, to see what your numbers actually look like outside a place like this."

Marcus stopped bouncing his knee. "So I might not have anything?"

"You might not. Or you might. I can't prognosticate from one nervous number in a white building." She heard herself say it and did not wince; her mother had always claimed she'd be a doctor because of sentences like that, though Alexandra suspected the real reason was that she liked knowing the names of things, all of them, even the useless ones.

Reyes came over and looked at the card. She asked Marcus what he'd eaten that day and whether he'd run up the hill to the infirmary, and Alexandra listened and understood that she was watching the same problem from another angle: a single reading was not a fact about a body, it was a fact about a body in a moment. The word for what the campers called the "fun run" was an oxymoron as far as Alexandra was concerned, and Marcus had done it twice that morning, which had not helped his numbers or his mood.

Reyes told Marcus to have his mother take his pressure twice at home this week, once relaxed and once after dinner, and to bring the numbers to his own doctor in the fall. She told Alexandra to take the blood pressure of every counselor who volunteered this afternoon, sitting, after five minutes of rest, and to write down where each reading happened. "Same arm, same time of day, same room if you can manage it," she said. "You'll start to see which numbers are about the person and which are about the circumstances. It takes longer than two weeks to learn the difference."

That afternoon Alexandra set up a folding table outside the dining hall, between the canteen and the volleyball court. The first counselor to volunteer was the drama instructor, whose readings were so consistently, stubbornly normal that Alexandra began to distrust them out of pure contrariness. The second was the archery teacher, an obstreperous man who refused to sit still and complained that the cuff was a form of censorship, and his numbers came back high both times. She wrote them down anyway, and in the notes column she put: "would not stop talking, may not be representative," which was the most honest sentence she had written all day.

By dinner she had eight cards. The readings ranged from textbook to alarming, and she knew that tomorrow Reyes would ask her what the pattern was, and she did not yet have an answer that fit them all. She had a stack of numbers, a bruise on her thumb from the pump bulb, and Marcus's mother's cuff somewhere across the lake, waiting to tell a different story than the one the infirmary had told.

Marcus came by the table on his way to the evening campfire. "My mom texted," he said. "She's bringing the cuff up on visitors' day."

"Good," Alexandra said. "Take it that morning before you do anything else." She squared the cards against the table edge. "Then we'll see what your heart does when nobody's watching."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Computing a binary search's midpoint as (low + high) / 2 can overflow on very large arrays; writing low + (high - low) / 2 gives the same middle without the overflow.
story:
Devin's basement smelled like carpet older than both of them and microwave popcorn someone had abandoned halfway. Joshua set his laptop on the ping-pong table, which served as desk, lunch counter, and, in a pinch, drum kit. Regionals were in eleven days, and the two of them had exactly one problem left to solve before they could call themselves ready.

"You wrote the search yourself?" Devin asked, sliding into a folding chair.

"Last night. It's a binary search, obviously. You split the range in half, check the middle, throw away the half that can't contain the answer, and do it again. Twenty guesses gets you through a million numbers." Joshua turned the laptop so Devin could see. "The linear search they teach you first walks the whole array from the front. Fine for a grocery list, embarrassing for anything sorted and serious."

"I know what it is. I asked whether you wrote it." Devin spun a ping-pong ball on his fingertip, lost it under the couch, and didn't seem to mind. "Because you wrote the union-find thing yourself and it had a bug you called a feature."

"That was a colloquialism. I said 'personality.'" Joshua pulled up the test harness and ran it. All forty cases went green. He leaned back with the particular smugness of a seventeen-year-old whose code has just passed a test he also wrote. "Behold."

"Run the big one," Devin said. He was already digging through a folder of competition datasets, past years' problem sets, some of them with inputs so large they had to ship zipped. He dropped one onto the laptop. "That one. Two hundred million elements."

Joshua ran it. The program ate a quarter of the array's worth of memory, found the search function, and stopped with a runtime error where the answer should have been. The two of them stared at the red line the way you stare at a door that has always opened before.

"Works on the tests," Joshua said, which was the kind of sentence that sounded like a defense and was actually a confession.

"You tested it on twelve numbers and forty numbers and numbers small enough to count on your hands. Then you threw two hundred million at it and it fell over. Overflow is endemic to competitive programming, everyone does this once." Devin pulled his chair around and scrolled to the search. He tapped one line with a pen he'd been using to stir tea. "There. That's your midpoint."

Joshua looked at the line. It read exactly the way the tutorial had read, exactly the way he'd copied it into his head at one in the morning: mid = (low + high) / 2. It had seemed so obviously correct that he'd never once wondered about it, which, he was beginning to understand, was the technical definition of the bugs that get you. He tried to imagine what the expression was actually doing, tried to reify the abstraction into a picture, and the picture was two enormous numbers being added together before anything got halved. "Okay," he said slowly. "Okay, I see it. If low and high are both huge, I add them first. I make something even huger, and then I divide."

"So don't add them first," Devin said, as if it were the most obvious instruction in the world, and then he stole the pen back and drank the tea he had been using it on, which was a mistake they would both hear about.

Joshua deleted the line and retyped it: mid = low + (high - high) / 2. Devin cleared his throat. Joshua looked up, looked down, and fixed it to low + (high - low) / 2, computing the distance between the endpoints and adding only half of that back to the low end. Same middle, none of the monster number in between. His ears went warm. "You watched me type that."

"I watched you type that," Devin confirmed, delighted.

They ran the dataset again. This time the program went quiet for a moment and then printed the index, correct, and the two of them sat in the basement half-light with the popcorn smell and the dead ping-pong ball somewhere under the couch, and Joshua felt the specific pleasure of a thing that had been broken and now was not. He thought about how he'd learned the search as a beautiful idea, halving and halving, and how the beauty had made him lazy about the arithmetic underneath it, and he understood that he'd have to hold both of those at once from now on: the elegance and the dumb, literal addition of two very large integers. Whether he'd actually learned that lesson or only believed he had, he couldn't yet say. He suspected the next eleven days would let him know.

"So explain it to me," Devin said, folding his arms like a bad actor playing a judge. "Like I'm the judge. Why is your search better than a linear one on sorted data?"

"Because the linear search looks at every element in order until it finds the target, and mine eliminates half the remaining range with each comparison. On two hundred million elements, you're talking about a handful of steps against, potentially, all of them." Joshua paused. "And I compute the midpoint as low plus high minus low, divided by two, which is the same middle without adding two giant bounds together first."

"The same middle without the overflow," Devin said, and held out his fist.

Joshua bumped it, then reached over and ran the big dataset one more time, just to watch the answer appear again, like a card trick he could finally do twice.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: A binary search of one million sorted items needs at most 20 comparisons, because halving one million twenty times leaves a single item.
story:
Cohen's grandfather was recuperating from knee surgery in the back bedroom, which was why Cohen had the kitchen table to himself all afternoon, along with a laptop, a plate of oatmeal cookies, and his grandmother's recipe box. The box held four hundred index cards in alphabetical order, cardamom to zwieback, and Cohen had promised his friend Priya a demonstration by dinner.

The problem had started two nights ago in a group chat. Priya had claimed she could find any word in a million-entry list faster than Cohen could, checking one entry at a time from the beginning. Cohen had said that was insane, that she'd be old before she got halfway, and she had sent back a single line: "Halve it, genius." He had looked up what she meant, found something called binary search, and understood it the way you understand a map of a city you've never walked. He needed to build it, break it, and then explain it in his own words, because their computer science teacher had announced that the first one to teach a concept convincingly to someone else got to skip the quiz.

So he had come to his grandparents' house, where the surgery meant quiet, and the recipe box meant data. He wrote a small program first: a list of one million numbers, sorted, and a function that held the whole procedure in one tidy package, taking the list and the target and returning an index. His textbook called this encapsulation, hiding the steps inside a named unit so you could use it without thinking about the parts, and Cohen liked that the word also described his grandmother's medicine cabinet, each drawer labeled, nobody needing to see inside.

Then he ran the experiment. He made the program count its own comparisons. Searching the million numbers one at a time from the front took, in the worst case, a million comparisons, and Cohen watched the counter climb so slowly he got up and ate a cookie while it worked. Then he let the halving version run, and it finished before the cursor blinked: at most twenty comparisons, because halving one million twenty times leaves a single item. He ran it again with different targets. Never more than twenty. He sat very still for a moment, cookie in hand, smelling cardamom from the open box.

"Grandma," he called toward the hallway, "if I asked you to find a recipe, how would you do it?"

She came in wiping her hands on a towel. "Depends on what it starts with. For popovers I'd open near the middle, see I'd gone past them, and flip back toward the P's." She leaned over his screen. "Is that your grandfather's knee? It looks like an X-ray."

"It's a list of numbers. But that's what you do, right? You jump to the middle."

"Everything in this house is alphabetized because I don't have time to page through four hundred cards for a scone." She took a cookie and went back to the hallway, and Cohen wrote down what she'd said, almost word for word, in the notebook where he was drafting his explanation for Priya. The catch, which he'd discovered the hard way at two in the morning, was that it only worked sorted. He had fed the halving program a shuffled list and it had returned garbage, confidently, with no error message at all, and that bothered him more than a crash would have.

At five o'clock Priya called. "Ready to lose?"

"I already won," Cohen said, and he told her the number. "A binary search of one million sorted items needs at most twenty comparisons. You'd need a million doing it your way."

"Twenty." He could hear her doing something with a pen, tapping it against a phone case. "Wait, no. Twenty?"

"Because halving one million twenty times leaves a single item. I counted it. I didn't believe it either."

There was a pause long enough that he could hear his grandfather's radio through the wall, tuned to the ballgame. "That can't be right for unsorted lists, though," Priya said.

"It isn't. That's the part I want to say in class on Monday. It only beats checking in order if the data's sorted, and the sorting costs something too, and I don't know yet whether that cost is worth paying if you're only searching once. I haven't worked that out." He turned the recipe box toward the window light, squared its cards, and slid the whole thing closer to the laptop, four hundred pieces of putative evidence for Monday morning, when he would line them up on the classroom desk and let someone call out a card.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Thomas Carlyle's The French Revolution: A History, published in 1837, stressed the moral choices of individuals rather than impersonal historical forces.
story:
Olivier had promised himself he would start the historiographical essay on Monday, and by Thursday evening he had produced a single sentence, deleted it, and produced it again. The prompt wanted him to trace how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800, which meant reading historians arguing with dead historians arguing with the event itself. He sat at the kitchen table with his laptop open and four tabs of PDFs, none of them closer than a decade old, and his grandmother's voice came from the hallway asking whether he wanted to come along on Saturday after all.

Saturday meant the drive to Grand-père's house to help clear the study, a project his mother had been postponing since the funeral in March. Olivier had refused twice already, citing the essay. "Then bring the essay," his grandmother said, holding up the car keys. "There's a desk there. It's quiet. It's quieter than here, anyway, and the wifi barely exists, which you claim to want."

The house smelled of pipe tobacco that had faded into the plaster years ago. Grand-père had been a history teacher, the kind whose shelves bent under gilt spines. Olivier set up at the desk under the window while his grandmother attacked the filing cabinets downstairs, and by three o'clock the light had gone crepuscular enough that he had to switch on the green lamp. He had an outline, sort of. Marxists saw the Revolution as the bourgeoisie toppling feudalism; revisionists said class was never the engine; post-revisionists said the Revolution invented politics itself. He could recite all this. What he couldn't do was make the paragraphs care about any of it.

He was reaching for a book to prop the laptop when he found it: The French Revolution: A History, by Thomas Carlyle, published, said the yellowed title page, in 1837. Grand-père's marginalia ran down the margins in three different inks across what must have been decades. Olivier opened it at random and hit a wall of prose like a thunderstorm. Carlyle wrote as if the Revolution were a morality play, a "dread chasseur" hunting France toward doom, every page pitched at the volume of an organ. Olivier, who had been raised on academic prose that apologized for having a pulse, read a paragraph, then read it again, and laughed out loud at the sheer nerve of it.

He carried the book downstairs to show his grandmother, who was kneeling among folders with a dust mask pushed up on her forehead. "It was his favorite," she said. "He told students it was wrong about everything and magnificent anyway. Carlyle cared about the moral choices of individuals, he used to say. Not impersonal historical forces. Everyone was a soul deciding, minute by minute." She peeled off a glove and turned the pages carefully. "He underlined the same passage for forty years, look."

She tapped a sentence heavy with double lines, in the oldest ink. Olivier read it and felt the strange sensation of a Victorian shouting at him from 1837 about men and their choices while his outline, upstairs, sat organized around structures and forces. He asked whether Grand-père had agreed with Carlyle. "Agreed?" she said. "He argued with him at dinner. He'd say, Your Carlyle made it all dependent on whether some deputy had his coffee. Grand-père would say, better that than a history where nobody is ever responsible."

Back at the desk, Olivier spread his outline beside the old book and tried a different approach. He drafted a paragraph in which Carlyle's dramatic style became the argument itself: the theater of the prose asserted that what mattered in history was what individuals chose, and the plainer twentieth-century historians, with their economic causes and their careful footnotes, were answering him in a flat voice, the way you answer someone who has shouted. He wrote a sentence connecting this to the Marxist reading, then a sentence complicating it, then deleted half of both. His phone buzzed. His grandmother, texting from the kitchen: "Tea. Also I found the fondue set. Did you know we had a fondue set."

At dinner she asked what the essay was arguing, and he said he wasn't sure yet whether it argued anything, which she said was the most honest thing a historian had ever told her at her own table. He described the problem: Carlyle made you feel that history was a series of souls deciding, and the later historians made you feel it was a river that would have run downhill regardless, and the more he read the more both seemed partly right and neither seemed complete, and his professor wanted a thesis, a single defensible line, by Monday. "So give her the line you actually have," his grandmother said, spooning out the last of the rice.

Later, at the desk, Olivier typed a draft thesis that he suspected would survive exactly one more revision: that the historiography of the Revolution had been a long argument about how much of history is chosen and how much is endured, and that Carlyle, writing in 1837, had stated one side so extravagantly that everyone after him was partly defining themselves against his voice. He appended a paragraph admitting where the essay stayed uncertain, that he couldn't tell whether responsibility and impersonal force were competing explanations or just two vocabularies for the same events. Then he saved the file twice, out of superstition, and sat looking at the book in the lamplight, at the three colors of ink marching down the margin, and at his own pencil resting beside it, waiting for the morning.
